title: What did you do yesterday? — the past tense
goal: Talk about what has already happened — and accept something English never does: the Slovenian past tense agrees with the GENDER and NUMBER of the doer, so the same sentence is said differently by a man and a woman.
bekal: building the past tense: *sem* + a verb ending in *-l*
putting *sem* in second place — *Delal sem*, not *Sem delal*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kaj si delal med vikendom?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in the cafeteria. Maja asks about the weekend, and Budi discovers that one past-tense form can mean two things at once.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: What did you do at the weekend?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bil sem v Bohinju. Z Evo sva hodila v hribe.
lines.id: I was in Bohinj. Eva and I went hiking in the mountains.
lines.literal: was-m I-am in Bohinj. with Eva we-two-are walked-du to mountain-pl.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Sta hodila? Torej sta bila dva.
lines.id: "Hodila"? So there were two of you.
lines.literal: you-two-are walked-du? so you-two-are been-du two.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja. Za tri bi bilo hodili.
lines.id: Yes. With three it would be "hodili".
lines.literal: yes. for three would been-n walked-pl.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Točno. In Eva? Kaj je rekla ona?
lines.id: Exactly. And Eva? What did she say?
lines.literal: exactly. and Eva? what she-is said-f she?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rekla je, da je bilo zelo lepo.
lines.id: She said it was really lovely.
lines.literal: said-f she-is, that it-is been-n very lovely.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Rekla, ne rekel — ker je ženska.
lines.literal: said-f, not said-m — because she-is woman.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ampak rekla je tudi za dva moška!
lines.id: But "rekla" is also used for two men!
lines.literal: but said-f is also for two man-du!

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Ja, oblika je ista. Glagol pove, katera je.
lines.id: Yes, the form is identical. The helping verb tells you which.
lines.literal: yes, form is same. verb tells, which is.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Je rekla — ena. Sta rekla — dva.
lines.id: "Je rekla" — one person. "Sta rekla" — two people.
lines.literal: she-is said — one. they-two-are said — two.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Bravo. Now you understand the past tense.

notes: **The past tense is built from two pieces: *sem* and a verb ending in *-l*.** *Delal sem* = I worked (yesterday). The first piece marks who did it; the second marks their **gender and number**. English marks neither, so this part really is new.

**The ending *-l* is pronounced like *w*.** *Delal* = **DAY-low**, *bil* = **beew**, *rekel* = **RAY-kuhw**, *šel* = **shuhw**. This is the pronunciation rule you'll use most in the whole course — and precisely because the past tense is everywhere, it's the one that makes you sound natural fastest.

**Rekla is two forms that happen to be twins.** It means "(a woman) said" **and** "(two men) said". The word itself gives no clue — the helping verb gives it away: *je rekla* (one woman) versus *sta rekla* (two men). The same twinning happens with *rekli*: two women, or three or more men.

**Sem may never stand at the start of a sentence.** It's a clitic, and clitics sit in second place — so *Delal sem*, not *Sem delal*. If you want to start with a time word, that becomes the first word: *Včeraj **sem** delal*. If you want to start with the doer: *Jaz **sem** delal*.

**Bilo je lepo — the neuter form for things with no gender.** When you're not talking about a particular person or thing, Slovenian uses the neuter: *Bilo je lepo* (it was lovely), *Bilo je težko* (it was hard), *Bilo je vroče* (it was hot). Sentences like these are very common and very cheap — there's nothing to adjust.

grammars.title: Pretekli čas — the past tense, at a glance
body: Here is the verb *delati* (work) in all its past-tense forms. The left column shows the doer, the next the helping verb plus the ending that agrees with the doer.
after: Four endings, that's all: **-l** (one man), **-la** (one woman *or* two men), **-li** (two women *or* three or more including a man), **-le** (three or more women). The neuter *-lo* is for things with no gender: *Bilo je lepo*.

The negative replaces the helping verb instead of adding a separate *ne*: **nisem delal**, *nisi delal*, *ni delal*, *nisva delala*, *nismo delali*. Note that *nisem* is not a clitic, so it **can** stand at the start: *Nisem delal.*

grammars.title: Past forms that don't play by the rules
body: Most verbs simply swap *-ti* for *-l*: *delati* → *delal*, *govoriti* → *govoril*, *kuhati* → *kuhal*. The dozen most common ones aren't that polite — and those are exactly the ones you'll say every day.
after: Notice the hidden pattern: the male form often slips in an *e* that vanishes again in the female form — *rekel* → *rekla*, *šel* → *šla*, *mogel* → *mogla*. That *e* is just a weak "uh" sound that appears so the word can be pronounced; once a vowel follows, it's no longer needed.

*Šel* and *šla* are worth learning before all the others: they're used for every change of place, and they're the past forms Slovenians say most often. *Šel sem domov* (I went home), *Šla je v šolo* (she went to school).

blocks.text: The past tense becomes useful as soon as you can string three sentences together. The examples below are in the male form; women simply add *-a* to every word ending in *-l*.

Notice *Nisem imel časa* — two rules at once: the helping verb becomes *nisem*, and *čas* becomes *časa* because the sentence is negative. It's one of the sentences adults everywhere say most, so learn it whole.

Places that might come up in your story: **Bled** (the lake with an island in the middle), **Bohinj** (a bigger, quieter lake), **Piran** (a Venetian-style seaside town), **Postojnska jama** (a cave), and **Triglav** (the highest mountain, which local custom says every Slovenian must climb once in a lifetime).
Because the helping verb is a clitic, its position depends on what you put in front. The four orders below are all correct and all mean the same — the only difference is what gets the emphasis.
There's just one practical rule: **whatever you put first, *sem* follows right after it**. If there's nothing in front, the verb itself becomes the first word and *sem* follows it.

blocks.title: The four most common mistakes
items: *Sem delal* at the start of a sentence — wrong. A clitic never opens a sentence. The right way: *Delal sem.*
A woman saying *delal* — wrong, though always understood. The right form is *delala*. This is the mistake people notice fastest.
Forgetting to change *sem* to *nisem* in a negative sentence and saying *ne sem delal*. That form doesn't exist.
Reading the *-l* ending as an "l". *Delal* is pronounced **DAY-low**, not "de-lal".

blocks.text: And one piece of good news: Slovenian has only **one** past tense. There's no difference between "I worked", "I have worked", "I was working" and "I had worked" — they're all *delal sem*. The finer differences come from the choice of verb, and that's what unit 14 is about.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right past-tense form.
Wave review — unit 10. Translate into Slovenian without looking back at the unit.
items: We have an exam on Friday.
Next week I'm going to Maribor.

answers: Delal sem doma. — Delala sem doma. — Šel sem v hribe. — Pila sem kavo. — Midva sva hodila. — Kuhale smo.

Kaj si delal včeraj? — Včeraj sem bil doma. — Šel sem v hribe. — Bilo je zelo lepo. — Nisem imel časa. — Prišel sem pozno.
